articleTitle: Simulator design in advance of plant build
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Operator Training Simulators
abstract: Modern quality assurance practices together with advances in simulation technology that enable the rapid and efficient generation of plant specific models and operator interfaces have introduced the option of designing and constructing plant specific training simulators considerably in advance of plant build. The consequent establishment of simulator based plant specific training may be mandatory and certainly appears to have many benefits to the end user both in terms of the direct training outcome, such as plant availability, but also in direct support to the plant design and test activity. It does, however, require careful management and planning and a recognition that the capability of the final simulator is principally limited by the timing, quality and extent of the data supplied together with a clear view of the ultimate training duty.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Training simulators-quantification of benefits and lessons learnt: a user's perspective
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Operator Training Simulators
abstract: BP Chemicals has installed training simulators at four of its five major European locations. Three of these simulators were bought initially to train operators prior to commissioning and start up of major new plants. The other two were bought for general site training particularly where reinstrumentation is a significant feature. The total investment in these systems is significant and not surprisingly needed a thorough justification before funds were released. The primary justification for the simulators has been productivity. Improved operational safety also featured strongly, but productivity provided the quantifiable benefits. Other benefits identified are: licence to operate safely, plant design/operability, operator validation of training and publicity. Lessons learnt during the building, installing and using of the training simulators are also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The use of dynamic process models for operator training
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Operator Training Simulators
abstract: Control of production processes is increasingly becoming more important to make products of higher quality, to reduce waste of energy and materials, and to increase production flexibility. To improve the overall process performance, process operators require more insight in the behaviour of the process. Particularly, when changeovers frequently occur, or when the process often experiences disturbances, operators need to be able to understand and control the dynamic behaviour of the process. Developments in MIMO process modelling and model based control system design as well as developments in hardware have opened new perspectives for supervisory control. Model based controllers and fast real-time simulators can be implemented at the DCS level providing fast and accurate MIMO supervisory control or process simulation. The models underlying the control design can also be applied for training operators in the use of these supervisory controllers and for providing insight in the behaviour of the process.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Simulator training for nuclear reactor plant operators
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Operator Training Simulators
abstract: British Nuclear Fuels plc operate two nuclear power generating stations in the UK, each comprising four Magnox type reactors. The reactors at both stations are fully protected by automatic shutdown systems which become effective upon irregularities in plant operating conditions. In addition to the provision of fully automated protection it is considered necessary to train operators to recognise potential plant problems. A decision was taken to upgrade the resource for operator training. In particular a simulator or emulator was required to enable operators to practice fault diagnosis and rectification procedures which might be experienced during 'once in a lifetime' fault scenarios. Two were required one for each station which would take account of any minor differences in plants and operating strategies. Potential solutions were examined and a requirement specification was used to assess them. The result was that Marconi Simulation was asked to provide a compact simulation training solution.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Current application of simulators in the process industries and future trends
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Operator Training Simulators
abstract: The application of dynamic simulators in industry is discussed, based on ABB Simcon's experience of executing over 80 projects throughout the world. The bulk of this experience is based on developing operator training simulators though other simulators are considered. The author discusses the current application of these simulators in the process industries and identifies trends which may indicate the way this technology will be used in the future. The use of training simulators is quite widespread within certain process industry sectors such as refining, petrochemical and oil and gas. Due to advances in technology and a wider awareness of the benefits these simulators are increasingly used for engineering and operations purposes. In the future the distinction between training and engineering simulators can be expected to be less clear. It is thought that soon a single tool will be available to enable a simulator to be used from conceptual design through to operations support.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Operator Training Simulators
abstract: Dynamic simulation is undoubtedly one of the most effective types of on-the-job training which you can get, away from the workplace-but in a depressing number of industries, it has received a surprisingly bad press. Most industries naturally have their own pet horror stories but, on closer examination, these invariably stem from basic flaws in the selection or utilisation procedures rather than from some native fault in the simulator itself. The author looks to redress the balance by examining in some detail: why a simulator is used, what types of simulator are available, how simulators are used in different industries, how to buy a simulator and what simulators are, and should be, used for.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Cost effective architecture for real-time simulators
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Operator Training Simulators
abstract: The importance of process simulation and especially simulation in real-time, is becoming increasingly apparent to industry. A real-time dynamic simulator can have various applications such as assessment of new plant operating conditions, operator training and safety analysis. Although there are many steady state flow sheet simulators only few dynamic simulators are available with generic applications. The limitations of the existing generic products and the high cost of customised simulators have created a barrier suppressing the commitment of medium sized firms towards this technology. However, recent advances in processor technology have made is possible to greatly reduce the cost of real-time simulation environments. The author provides an overview of a cost effective high-performance architecture for real-time simulation applications, i.e. multiprocessor architecture.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
